clue.text: Dejected banana-skin victim

definitions.meaning: downcast, with the jaw drooping in gloom
read as two words, a man who has slipped and gone down: a fellow who has taken a tumble

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer into CHAP (a man) and FALLEN, the comic fate of someone who treads on a banana skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapfallen literally means with the jaw hanging, a picture of dismay, hence downcast; a chap fallen is a man who has tripped over.

clue.text: Where wives might be about fifty, in New York

definitions.note: the definition names a place found in New York

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the wives' quarters are put around the other piece

parts.note: a harem is the quarters for a sultan's wives
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Wives in New York are around fifty years old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts HAREM around L.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlem is a district of Manhattan.

clue.text: A brave enemy making him look so scared?

definitions.text: A brave enemy making him look so scared?

parts.words: A brave enemy making him look so scared
parts.note: a brave is a Native American warrior; his foe is a white settler, named for a complexion that also suggests fright

explanation.surface: A frightening foe of a courageous warrior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave' is a noun, a Native American warrior; the old Western term for his white enemy also describes a face blanched with fear.
explanation.definitionFit: Paleface was the name given in Westerns to white settlers by Native Americans; a pale face also shows fear.

clue.text: British queen consumed one port in Egypt

indicators.note: consumed means swallowed, so the queen holds the other piece inside

parts.note: Alexandra was the queen of Edward VII
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A British queen ate something in an Egyptian port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumed' puts I inside ALEXANDRA, Edward VII's queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandria is the great Mediterranean harbour city of Egypt.

clue.text: Birthday present?

parts.note: not a gift on an anniversary, but what is ready for the day a baby is born

explanation.surface: A gift for someone's birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birthday' means the actual day of birth, so the present is the set of clothes made ready for a newborn.
explanation.definitionFit: A layette is the outfit of clothes and linen prepared for a newborn baby.

clue.text: Jack heard in church

definitions.note: the definition names a part found in a church

indicators.note: heard means spoken, so the card's name is replaced by one sounding the same

parts.note: the jack in a pack of cards is also called the knave

explanation.surface: A man named Jack is overheard during a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' gives a word sounding like KNAVE, the card also called the jack, whose K is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: The nave is the main body of a church, where the congregation sits.

clue.text: Certainly not an aimless pastime

parts.note: a hobby that is far from purposeless, read literally as one that demands taking aim

explanation.surface: A hobby that has a real purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aimless' looks like purposeless, but it means without aiming, and a gun sport is all about aiming.
explanation.definitionFit: Firing at game or targets is a sport which requires taking aim.

clue.text: Characteristic of the clever Birkenhead justice

parts.note: read as Birken's head, the first letter B
rightness is the quality of being just

explanation.surface: Cleverness and fairness typify Lord Birkenhead, the brilliant judge.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 'Birkenhead' as 'Birken head': its head is B. The surface recalls F. E. Smith, Lord Birkenhead, a famously clever Lord Chancellor; Birkenhead is also a town on Merseyside.
explanation.definitionFit: Clever people are said to be bright, so quick wit marks them.

clue.text: One securing a purchase by a fluke?

definitions.text: One securing a purchase by a fluke?

parts.words: One securing a purchase by a fluke
parts.note: the surface suggests a lucky buyer, but a purchase is a firm grip and a fluke is the barbed blade of a ship's mooring device that digs into the seabed

explanation.surface: Someone who lands a bargain purely by luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' means grip and 'fluke' is the pointed arm that bites into the sea floor, so the lucky shopper is really a ship's mooring hook.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's heavy hook holds fast by driving its flukes into the seabed, gaining a purchase there.

clue.text: Large number wave to youth leader-that's funny

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for five hundred
a roller is a long heavy wave breaking on a shore

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so the opening letter of youth is taken

explanation.surface: Someone sees a crowd waving at the head of a youth group and finds it comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large number' is D, Roman 500.
explanation.definitionFit: Drollery is comic humour or a whimsical jest, something that amuses.

clue.text: Service, for a price of course, on garage opening

parts.note: evens is a betting price at a racecourse, odds of one to one
taken as written

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so garage gives its initial

explanation.surface: A churchgoer muses on prices and a new garage opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' is a racecourse, where EVENS is a bookmaker's price.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is the Anglican evening prayer service.

clue.text: Pip's follower in the book ?

definitions.meaning: in old signallers' alphabet P was Pip and M was ..., so p.m. was spoken as Pip followed by this word

explanation.walkthrough: Signallers once said PIP EMMA for p.m. (afternoon); Pip is not the Great Expectations hero here. Austen's novel bears the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Signalese gave the letter M as Emma, the word after Pip in p.m.; Austen wrote a novel titled with that heroine's name.

clue.text: Completely covered and finished, including an hour's break

indicators.note: including means holding inside, so the finished word takes the other piece within it

parts.note: ended means finished

indicators.note: to break something is to shatter it, so the letters of hour's are rearranged

explanation.surface: A job is wrapped up, with an hour's break taken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' rearranges HOUR'S as SHROU; 'including' puts that in ENDED, after EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enshrouded is wrapped all over, as in a burial cloth.

clue.text: Perhaps Darwin gets a note — it's odd

parts.note: in music a natural is a note neither sharp nor flat

indicators.note: odd means strange or out of order, so the letters of it's are rearranged

explanation.surface: Darwin is told a musical note sounds strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' rearranges IT'S into IST.
explanation.definitionFit: Darwin was a famous student of plants and animals, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: He and his mates work on parallel lines

definitions.text: He and his mates work on parallel lines

parts.words: He and his mates work on parallel lines
parts.note: parallel lines are the two rails of a track, so this worker maintains the permanent way

explanation.surface: A worker and his colleagues follow similar policies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parallel lines' suggests geometry or similar approaches; it is the two rails of a track.
explanation.definitionFit: A railwayman is an employee of a railway, working on its track.

clue.text: Principal villain in Dickens ?

parts.note: principal means headmaster: the cruel schoolmaster of Dotheboys Hall in Nicholas Nickleby

explanation.surface: Asking who is the chief baddie in Dickens's novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principal' looks like 'chief', but it means a head teacher: Wackford Squeers runs the brutal school in Nicholas Nickleby.
explanation.definitionFit: Wackford Squeers is the vicious headmaster of a Yorkshire school in Nicholas Nickleby.

clue.text: From Philip's farm to haunts of coot and hern, for instance

definitions.text: From Philip's farm to haunts of coot and hern, for instance

parts.words: From Philip's farm to haunts of coot and hern, for instance
parts.note: in Tennyson's poem The Brook the stream rises in the haunts of coot and hern and later flows by Philip's farm, so this journey goes against the current

explanation.surface: A ramble from a farm to a nature reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's The Brook begins 'I come from haunts of coot and hern' and passes Philip's farm lower down, so going from the farm to those haunts is moving toward the source.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling toward a river's source is going against its flow.

clue.text: A sanctimonious rascal in a canoe

parts.note: pi is a short informal word for piously self-righteous
a rogue is a scamp or rascal

explanation.surface: A self-righteous scoundrel paddles a canoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirogue is a dugout boat, the long narrow kind used in the Caribbean and Louisiana.

clue.text: Like the novelty of mixing oil with grain

indicators.note: mixing means stirring together, so the letters of oil and grain are rearranged

explanation.surface: A new recipe blends oil with grain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixing' rearranges OIL and GRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something new and fresh, never seen before, has this quality.

clue.text: The head takes kidnapper's spoils with a beam

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so The gives its initial

parts.note: a ransom is the payment a kidnapper demands

explanation.surface: A headmaster collects a kidnapper's loot and a beam of wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The head' is T, the first letter of 'The'.
explanation.definitionFit: A transom is a horizontal crossbar, as over a door or window.

clue.text: Plant is named in error-what's gone wrong ?

indicators.note: something gone wrong is out of order, so the letters of error and what's are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener mislabels a plant and asks what went wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone wrong' signals the anagram of ERROR WHAT'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Restharrow is a tough-rooted pea-family shrub of European grassland.

clue.text: Complaints of unopened accounts

indicators.note: unopened means without its opening, so the first letter is cut off

parts.note: bills are invoices or accounts

explanation.surface: Grumbles about bills left sealed in envelopes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unopened' drops the B of BILLS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ills are troubles or ailments, things one complains of.

clue.text: Noel is badly hurt

indicators.note: badly means in poor order, so the letters of Noel is are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Noel has been badly injured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' looks like it qualifies 'hurt', but it rearranges NOEL IS.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesion is a wound or injury to body tissue.

clue.text: Nuns are nothing unusual ? Nonsense!

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters are put in a strange order

parts.note: O, the zero figure, means nothing

explanation.surface: Someone insists there is nothing odd about nuns, and another scoffs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges NUNS ARE with O.
explanation.definitionFit: Unreason is a lack of sense or logic, so it means absurdity.

clue.text: Weapon used in first engagement?

indicators.note: the letters are found running inside the words first engagement

explanation.surface: A weapon fired in an opening battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used in' points to the letters spanning 'firST ENgagement'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sten was a light British submachine gun of the Second World War.

clue.text: Relating to meaning for many — it calls for a reversal

indicators.note: a reversal turns the whole string of pieces backwards

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a large number
taken as written
to call is to name, so calls gives names

explanation.surface: Someone muses that a word's meaning changes when it is turned round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a reversal' turns C+IT+NAMES backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Semantic means concerned with the sense of words.

clue.text: Pass the Spanish recess

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for the
an apse is a vaulted recess at the end of a church

explanation.surface: A traveller crosses a Spanish mountain pass into a hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that passes is said to go by in this way.

clue.text: Is it then a woman's place to separate the combatants ?

definitions.text: Is it then a woman's place to separate the combatants

parts.words: Is it then a woman's place to separate the combatants
parts.note: the strip between two armies has a name that says no men belong there, so the clue asks whether women own it

explanation.surface: A question about whether women should keep fighters apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The strip between front lines is called no man's land; the clue reads that literally as a place belonging to no men, hence perhaps to women.
explanation.definitionFit: No man's land is the disputed ground between two opposing trenches.
